items.title: Billy Taylor interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995
items.q: And from that point on, Jo was one of my mentors. So I mean he had a profound influence on my career.

ctx.x: Well I was lucky, I was lucky, I grew up in Washington, D.C. and in growing up in Washington, D.C., all the big bands came to the Howard Theater. My father, who was a dentist, had an office around the corner, literally around the corner from the theater. My grandfather’s church was almost adjacent to the theater. So much of my family, the things that I was legitimately in place for, was close to this theater, where all of the great artists played. Where Duke Ellington, where Count Basie, where Jimmie Lunceford,…

mean I was, I had the local, like at Virginia State we had a band that was the school band. It was an extracurricular activity. It wasn’t something the school sanctioned, but it was a dance band and a bunch of kids, and we had a faculty advisor, and it was a very fine musician, a guy named Solomon Phillips, who taught me to arrange and do some other things. But the Count Basie’s band was playing one nighters in Virginia. And they came through town. Well I mean we had all the Basie arrangements and we had, you…

You know I want to ask you something about that. Because you know many of the musicians that we have interviewed have said the same thing. They said at some point early on in their careers, someone had faith in them and they said okay I’ll give you a chance. I’ll let you sit in. Or you meet that one person that you may be even intimidated by their status but they give you a chance. You know? And that’s wonderful. I’d like to see more of that in the school systems.

items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: this was in my quartet days so I had Mondell Lowe on guitar by that time, I had Jo Jones on drums

ctx.x: Boogie Woogie in the left hand and bebop in the right hand, so that’s what the… one thing was called Taylor Made, and I don’t remember the titles now. I’ll find them for you and let you know what the titles are. But there were four… Down That Dream was one of the ballads that I played and it was a quartet. It was piano, bass, and drums, and guitar. I don’t remember who I used on the date because John Collins wasn’t available to me and I don’t remember who the trio was at that time but I’ll find out. I went…

you will be taken to a New York nightclub. This was one of the New York nightclubs. So we’d be right in the middle of the show and the door would come open and 20 or 30 people would walk in. You know, they’re walking around, aw, New York nightclub, wow, and they’re talking and everything. So Artie Shaw went nuts with all this kind of… he didn’t like that at all. But it was good quintet. We rehearsed over at his house. He was an excellent musician… because we were playing bebop by that time so I had written some…

I really loved to play with in Birdland. While we were working in Birdland, Quincy Jones made a record… had this concept and this is very early on in the days of layering or multi-taping or whatever the…

items.q: Then I stayed there with Billy Taylor, John Collins, Lloyd Troutman.

ctx.x: union; can I pay these people more?" Then I stayed there with Billy Taylor, John Collins, Lloyd Troutman. They built the Embers because of Billy but they kept Billy at the Down Beat, sent Billy over there with streamers on... break

Just take a break and relax for a bit. Hey, Jo, I'm going to play some Teddy Wilson, Jo Jones, and Milt Hinton. Can't remember what year we did this in but we were doing a television show at CBS called "On a Saturday Afternoon", called the Teddy Wilson Hour and then we made an album with it for Norman Granz. Let's listen to some of that.
